questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] a collaborative CRUD board with live updates and offline edits (jsprojectlearn, content/modules/system-design-for-crud.md). Scenario: a shared task board for warehouse shift teams. 600 sites each have one board that 10 to 25 people edit from tablets; together they make about 40,000 task edits a day (create, retitle, mark done, delete). Wi-Fi dead zones mean a tablet can be offline for up to 45 minutes and must keep working, and a supervisor expects a colleague's change to appear on screen within 2 seconds. Run the interview script before you look: rough numbers and what they rule out, where the truth about a board lives, how writes and live updates travel, what a tablet does with its own edits before the server confirms them, what it does while offline, and how it catches up after a reconnect. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w2] Does the arithmetic and draws the conclusion: 40,000 edits a day is under one write a second on average, so even a peak fifty times higher is a small load for one database. Scale is not the hard part here; keeping 600 boards consistent across flaky tablets is.
keyPoints.quote: Enough to know whether one database will do.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Names one place where a board's truth lives: the server keeps a numbered log of changes, every tablet rebuilds its view by applying those changes in the server's order (its own edits included, coming back through the same pipe), and that shared order is what makes every screen end up identical.

[w2] Gives each direction its own channel: edits go up as ordinary HTTP requests, where they are validated and rejected with a proper error shape, and the socket only carries changes down to the tablets; clients never write over it.

[w3] Catch-up after a reconnect needs no special protocol: the tablet sends the highest version it has applied, and the server first replays every logged change after that number, then continues with live ones, so a dropped connection loses nothing.

[w3] Own edits show instantly as provisional rows, each tagged with a random label sent along with the write; when the server's change comes back carrying that label, it replaces the provisional row in place instead of adding a second copy of it.

[w3] Offline, the tablet's own copy is what the screen shows, and every edit also goes into an outbox that collapses as it grows: repeated edits to one task merge into a single operation in its original queue position, a delete drops the edits queued before it, and the merged operation takes a new id so a sync already in flight cannot acknowledge away the newer typing.
[w2] A deleted task stays behind as a dated tombstone, because a merge with the server's copy that saw 'the server has it and I do not' would otherwise bring it back.
[w2] Finds the race before drawing boxes: two people change the same task, one of them while offline, and the design has to say which change survives and whether the loser is told.
keyPoints.quote: Every design question hides one race.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the first month on the warehouse floor, on a build shaped like the course's collaborative todo server and offline-notes client: the API process is redeployed at 14:00 in the middle of a shift; a tablet comes back after 45 offline minutes with 30 queued edits, and its clock runs 4 minutes fast; a flaky link drops the response to a 'create task' request and the tablet sends it again; the team adds a second API instance behind the load balancer; and a supervisor deletes a task that a tablet had edited while offline. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The redeploy freezes every open board without an error: the log, the tasks and the version counter live in the process's memory, so the new process numbers changes from 1 again; tablets reconnect asking for changes after version 40, get none, and discard every new change as already seen, while their own new tasks wait for a confirmation that never arrives. A durable log, plus a log identity that changes on reset so a tablet knows to rebuild, prevents it.

[w3] The fast tablet wins conflicts it should lose: last-write-wins compares timestamps taken from each device's own clock (kept monotonic per tab, never corrected), so edits made 4 minutes 'in the future' beat a supervisor's later change. Order conflicts by something the server assigns, or send the version each edit was based on.

[w3] The resent create makes a second task: the server mints a fresh id for every create request and uses the tablet's label only to recognise echoes, so a retry of a request that did succeed is indistinguishable from a new task. Let the tablet generate the task's id and make it the key, so the resend collides with the row that already exists and gets that row back.

[w2] The edits themselves replay safely: an offline operation sets field values and a timestamp rather than describing a change such as 'flip done', so applying the same queued batch twice leaves the same state. Keep operations in that set-the-value form; it is what makes the outbox retryable.

[w2] With a second instance, tablets connected to one process never hear about writes taken by the other, because each process holds its own log and its own set of open sockets. The log has to move to the database and the broadcast has to cross instances (a shared pub/sub channel) before the app tier can scale out.

[w2] The deleted task comes back: an offline edit stamped after the tombstone wins the merge, and applying an upsert clears the deleted flag. Decide the rule on purpose (a delete beats later edits, or an edit revives the task and says so), because the default here is silent resurrection.

[w1] Every rejected write makes that tablet download the entire history again (it rebuilds from version 0), which gets slower every day the log grows; a periodic snapshot with only the tail replayed keeps recovery cheap.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your sync design against the alternatives: server-ordered last-write-wins versus rejecting stale writes versus merging per field versus a CRDT; the server's log as the truth versus the device's copy as the truth; a WebSocket push versus polling an events endpoint; replaying the whole log versus a snapshot plus the tail; and server-assigned ids versus ids the client generates. Also say what you would not build yet. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Server-ordered last-write-wins is simple and total, and every screen agrees, but one person's intent is silently discarded; rejecting stale writes makes that loss visible, yet after 45 minutes offline it hands the user a stack of conflicts to resolve by hand; merging per field keeps both edits whenever different fields changed, at the price of tracking which fields each edit touched.
[w2] A CRDT or operational transform is only worth its library and payload cost for text several people type into at once; short task fields such as a title or a done flag do not need it.

[w3] The server's log as the truth gives one order that is easy to reason about, but the screen inherits the network's latency and failures; the device's copy as the truth makes every action instant and offline-proof, and costs merge rules, tombstones and an outbox that must be tested as carefully as the server.

[w2] Push meets the 2-second requirement at the cost of one open connection per tablet and a reconnect path to maintain; polling an events-after-version endpoint is stateless and easy to put behind a load balancer, but costs a request per tablet per interval and makes latency as long as the interval.

[w2] Replaying the whole log keeps rebuilding trivial (a fold over every change), and its cost grows with history; a snapshot plus the tail bounds that cost, at the price of a compaction job and of recording the version each snapshot was taken at.

[w2] Server-assigned ids are short and sequential but force the UI to wait: a provisional row cannot be toggled or deleted until its real id comes back. Client-generated ids allow creating offline and resending safely, at the cost of validating and scoping ids you did not mint and of a separate counter if people want readable task numbers.

[w1] Deferred on purpose at under one write a second: an event bus, separate services and an orchestration platform; two app instances, a managed Postgres and a shared pub/sub channel cover the requirement.
keyPoints.quote: A PaaS runs two instances and a managed database without it.
